additions.title: UK GDPR, Article 35: Data protection impact assessment
additions.quote: a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects relating to natural persons which is based on automated processing, including profiling
additions.why: The one risk screen UK statute does apply to AI that handles personal data: processing 'likely to result in a high risk' must be assessed first, and Art. 35(3) names three cases where that is always so, the first being automated evaluation and profiling on which significant decisions are based. A two-level screen for personal data processing, not a set of AI tiers; it says nothing about systems that use no personal data.

additions.title: Data protection impact assessments: When do we need to do a DPIA?
additions.locator: Section 'What does 'likely to result in a high risk' mean?'; section 'What does the ICO consider likely to result in high risk?' (innovative technology, denial of service)
additions.quote: are there features which point to the potential for high risk?
additions.why: The regulator's method for sorting processing into high risk or not: a high-level screen for red flags, with a published list under Art. 35(4). Use of innovative technology, AI included, needs an assessment when combined with another listed factor. Marked under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. No date printed on the page; the year given is the year it was read.

additions.title: Use of artificial intelligence in government (HC 612, Session 2023-24)
additions.quote: Only 30% of all 87 survey respondents reported that they had risk and quality assurance processes that explicitly incorporated AI risks
additions.why: Audit evidence on how far risk identification has got in practice. The same paragraph reports that almost half of the 32 bodies with deployed AI (15) kept no register of live AI use cases, so had nothing to classify. Limits: central government bodies only, self-reported survey (position as at autumn 2023), and a further 46% said they planned such processes.

additions.title: General principles for classification of high-risk AI systems (summary of the draft Commission guidelines)
additions.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
additions.quote: Check whether the AI system falls within one of the high-risk use cases in the sensitive areas listed in Annex III.
additions.why: The Commission's own six-step order for classifying a system: is it an AI system, what is its intended purpose, the Annex I route, the Annex III route, the Article 6(3) filter, and any transitional rule. A summary of DRAFT guidelines under Article 6(5): the Commission's library page dates the draft 19 May 2026 and the Service Desk still describes it as open to consultation until 23 July 2026, before formal adoption. Not binding, and may change on adoption. No date printed on this page.

additions.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 7: Amendments to Annex III
additions.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
additions.quote: to amend Annex III by adding or modifying use-cases of high-risk AI systems where both of the following conditions are fulfilled
additions.why: Why a classification cannot be done once and filed: the Commission may add or modify high-risk use cases by delegated act where a system in a listed area poses a risk equal to or greater than those already listed. This is the change a board would need to see coming, which is what the top level of the question asks. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

additions.title: AI Risk Assessment: A Scenario-Based, Proportional Methodology for the AI Act
additions.publisher: Digital Society (Springer Nature); C. Novelli, F. Casolari, A. Rotolo, M. Taddeo and L. Floridi
additions.quote: However, it lacks a clear methodology for the assessment of these risks in concrete situations.
additions.why: Peer-reviewed, open access. Argues that the AI Act's classes rest on broad application areas and so can misjudge the risk of a system in a particular setting, and proposes assessing risk by scenario (hazard, exposure, vulnerability, response). Supports recording reasons for a tier and not only the label. A proposal, not an empirical test; written against the text as it stood before the 2026 amendments.

additions.title: The AI risk repository: A meta-review, database, and taxonomy of risks from artificial intelligence
additions.publisher: arXiv (P. Slattery, A. K. Saeri, E. A. C. Grundy and others); stated on the page as published in Patterns (Cell Press), 2026
additions.quote: We systematically analyzed every major AI risk framework published to date-74 frameworks containing 1,725 distinct risks-and organized them into a unified system.
additions.why: A meta-review for the identification half of the question: the abstract reports 74 frameworks and 1,725 risks sorted by cause and by domain, and attributes 38% of risks to human decisions against 42% to the AI system. Useful as a checklist of what a classification method should have looked for. Authors' repository copy; the arXiv page says the paper has since been published in Patterns. Only the abstract page was read. The counts are of risks named in frameworks, not of incidents.

additions.title: OECD Framework for the Classification of AI Systems (OECD Digital Economy Papers No. 323)
additions.publisher: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
additions.locator: Executive summary, 'Key dimensions structure AI system characteristics and interactions'; Box 5 'AI risk-based approaches' (p.67)
additions.quote: The framework classifies AI systems and applications along the following dimensions
additions.why: International comparator. Classifies a system in its context of use along five dimensions (People & Planet, Economic Context, Data & Input, AI Model, Task & Output), which is a way to describe a bought-in tool before assigning it a tier. A descriptive policy tool, not a risk rating and not binding; it pre-dates general-purpose AI in wide use.

additions.title: NSW AI Assessment Framework
additions.locator: Opening section; notice 'The AIAF Platform is mandatory from 30 September 2026'
additions.quote: AI systems assessed as high or critical risk must be submitted to the AI Secretariat
additions.why: International comparator for the top level of the question: a government that requires every AI use case to be registered and risk-assessed, including procured systems, and sends the high and critical tiers to an independent review committee. New South Wales public sector only, under Circular DCS-2026-02; a self-assessment at the first stage. No date printed on the page.

rejected.title: ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 23894 and ISO/IEC 42005 standard pages
rejected.reason: HTTP 403 to automated reading on all three iso.org pages (42001, 77304, 42005). Not cited.

rejected.title: Canada, Directive on Automated Decision-Making (impact levels I to IV; Algorithmic Impact Assessment)
rejected.reason: HTTP 403 to automated reading; a guessed canada.ca address for the assessment tool returned 404. Not cited.

rejected.title: Colorado Senate Bill 24-205 (definition of high-risk artificial intelligence system)
rejected.reason: HTTP 403 to automated reading. Not cited.

rejected.title: Taking AI risks seriously: a new assessment model for the AI Act (AI & Society, 2023)
rejected.reason: Read. A short Open Forum column by the same authors; the full 2024 paper in Digital Society makes the same argument and was used instead.

rejected.title: Draft Commission guidelines on the classification of high-risk AI systems (library page)
rejected.reason: Read for the date (19 May 2026). The PDFs of the full draft are downloads and were not opened; the Service Desk summary page was cited and marked as a draft.

rejected.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 51: Classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
rejected.reason: Opened. Concerns providers of general-purpose models, not the systems an ordinary organisation classifies. Not relevant enough.

rejected.title: Model Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework, Second Edition (Singapore)
rejected.reason: Read. Its probability and severity of harm matrix (paragraphs 3.15-3.17) sets the level of human involvement, not a risk tier; used for the deployer controls criterion instead.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the brief. Two points of nuance: UK GDPR Art. 35(3) and the ICO's Art. 35(4) list are a statutory high-risk screen for personal data processing, which sits beside the brief's statement that UK law sets no AI risk tiers; and the Commission's Article 6(5) classification guidelines are still a draft (dated 19 May 2026; consultation closed 23 July 2026), so the brief is right to make no claim about them.
